The Jews' Inveterate Love of Idolatry.</title> <div sID="gen17720" type="x-p"/> The the Septuagint omits the first four verses, but other Greek versions have them.<div eID="gen17720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17721" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen17721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17722" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17723" type="x-p"/> 1. The first of the four clauses relates to the third, the second to the fourth, by alternate parallelism. The sense is: They are as keen after idols as if their propensity was "graven with an iron pen (<reference osisRef="Job.19.24">Job 19:24</reference>) on their hearts," or as if it were sanctioned by a law "inscribed with a diamond point" on their altars. The names of their gods used to be written on "the horns of the altars" (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.23">Ac 17:23</reference>). As the clause "on their hearts" refers to their inward propensity, so "on ... altars," the outward exhibition of it. Others refer "on the horns of ... altars" to their staining them with the blood of victims, in imitation of the Levitical precept (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.12">Ex 29:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.4.7">Le 4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.18">18</reference>), but "written ... graven," would thus be inappropriate.<div eID="gen17723" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17722" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17724" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">table of ... heart--</hi>which God intended to be inscribed very differently, namely, with His truths (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.3">Pr 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.3">2Co 3:3</reference>).<div eID="gen17724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17725" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your--</hi>Though "their" preceded, He directly addresses them to charge the guilt home to them in particular.<div eID="gen17725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17726" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9964"/><hi type="bold">2. children remember--</hi>Instead of forsaking the idolatries of their fathers, they keep them up (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.18">Jr 7:18</reference>). This is given as proof that their sin is "graven upon ... altars" (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.1">Jr 17:1</reference>), that is, is not merely temporary. They corrupt their posterity after them. Castalio less probably translates, "They remember their altars as (fondly as) they do their children."<div eID="gen17726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">groves--</hi>rather, "images of Astarte," the goddess of the heavenly hosts, represented as a sacred tree, such as is seen in the Assyrian sculptures (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.7">2Ki 21:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.18">2Ch 24:18</reference>). "Image of the grove." The Hebrew for "grove" is Asherah, that is, Assarak, Astarte, or Ashtaroth.<div eID="gen17727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the green trees--</hi>that is, near them: the sacred trees (idol symbols) of Astarte being placed in the midst of natural trees: "green trees" is thus distinguished from "groves," artificial trees. Henderson, to avoid taking the same Hebrew particle in the same sentence differently, "by ... upon" translates "images of Astarte on the green trees." But it is not probable that images, in the form of a sacred tree, should be hung on trees, rather than near them. <div eID="gen17728" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 17 Jr 17:1-27 . The Jews' Inveterate Love of Idolatry. The the Septuagint omits the first four verses, but other Greek versions have them. 1. The first of the four clauses relates to the third, the second to the fourth, by alternate parallelism. The sense is: They are as keen after idols as if their propensity was "graven with an iron pen ( Job 19:24 ) on their hearts," or as if it were sanctioned by a law "inscribed with a diamond point" on their altars. The names of their gods used to be written on "the horns of the altars" ( Ac 17:23 ). As the clause "on their hearts" refers to their inward propensity, so "on ... altars," the outward exhibition of it. Others refer "on the horns of ... altars" to their staining them with the blood of victims, in imitation of the Levitical precept ( Ex 29:12 ; Le 4:7 , 18 ), but "written ... graven," would thus be inappropriate. table of ... heart-- which God intended to be inscribed very differently, namely, with His truths ( Pr 3:3 ; 2Co 3:3 ). your-- Though "their" preceded, He directly addresses them to charge the guilt home to them in particular. 2. children remember-- Instead of forsaking the idolatries of their fathers, they keep them up ( Jr 7:18 ). This is given as proof that their sin is "graven upon ... altars" ( Jr 17:1 ), that is, is not merely temporary. They corrupt their posterity after them. Castalio less probably translates, "They remember their altars as (fondly as) they do their children." groves-- rather, "images of Astarte," the goddess of the heavenly hosts, represented as a sacred tree, such as is seen in the Assyrian sculptures ( 2Ki 21:7 ; 2Ch 24:18 ). "Image of the grove." The Hebrew for "grove" is Asherah, that is, Assarak, Astarte, or Ashtaroth. by the green trees-- that is, near them: the sacred trees (idol symbols) of Astarte being placed in the midst of natural trees: "green trees" is thus distinguished from "groves," artificial trees. Henderson, to avoid taking the same Hebrew particle in the same sentence differently, "by ... upon" translates "images of Astarte on the green trees." But it is not probable that images, in the form of a sacred tree, should be hung on trees, rather than near them.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9965"/><div sID="gen17729" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9965"/><hi type="bold">3. mountain--</hi>Jerusalem, and especially Zion and the temple.<div eID="gen17729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the field--</hi>As Jerusalem was surrounded by mountains (<reference osisRef="Ps.125.2">Psa 125:2</reference>), the sense probably is, Ye rely on your mountainous position (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.23">Jr 3:23</reference>), but I will make "My mountain" to become as if it were in a plain (field), so as to give thy substance an easy prey to the enemy [Calvin]. "Field" may, however, mean all Judea; it and "My mountain" will thus express the country and its capital. (Gesenius translates, "together with," instead of "in"; as the Hebrew is translated in <reference osisRef="Jer.11.19">Jr 11:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.5.6">Ho 5:6</reference>; but this is not absolutely needed), "the substance" of both of which God "will give to the spoil."<div eID="gen17730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy high places--</hi>corresponding in parallelism to "My mountain" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.11.9">Is 11:9</reference>), as "all thy borders," to "the field" (which confirms the view that "field" means all Judea).<div eID="gen17731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17732" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for sin--</hi>connected with high places" in English Version, namely, frequented for sin, that is, for idolatrous sacrifices. But <reference osisRef="Jer.15.13">Jr 15:13</reference> makes the rendering probable, "I will give thy substance ... to ... spoil ... on account of thy sin throughout all thy borders." <div eID="gen17732" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9968"/><div sID="gen17737" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9968"/><hi type="bold">6. heath--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Ps.102.17">Psa 102:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.11">Is 32:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.9">Ha 3:9</reference>, the Hebrew is translated, "bare," "naked," "destitute"; but as the parallel in <reference osisRef="Jer.17.8">Jr 17:8</reference> is "tree," some plant must be meant of which this is the characteristic epithet (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.6">Jr 48:6</reference>, Margin), "a naked tree." Robinson translates, "the juniper tree," found in the Arabah or Great Valley, here called "the desert," south of the Dead Sea. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9973"/><div sID="gen17749" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9973"/><hi type="bold">11. partridge--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.20">1Sa 26:20</reference>). Hebrew, korea, from a root, "to call," alluding to its cry; a name still applied to a bustard by the Arabs. Its nest is liable, being on the ground, to be trodden under foot, or robbed by carnivorous animals, notwithstanding all the beautiful manoeuvres of the parent birds to save the brood. The translation, "sitteth on eggs which it has not laid," alludes to the ancient notion that she stole the eggs of other birds and hatched them as her own; and that the young birds when grown left her for the true mother. It is not needful to make Scripture allude to an exploded notion, as if it were true. Maurer thinks the reference is to Jehoiakim's grasping cupidity (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.13-Jer.22.17">Jr 22:13-17</reference>). Probably the sense is more general; as previously He condemned trust in man (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.5">Jr 17:5</reference>), He now condemns another object of the deceitful hearts' trust, unjustly gotten riches (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.6">Psa 39:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.16">49:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.23">55:23</reference>).<div eID="gen17749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fool--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.23.5">Pr 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">Lu 12:20</reference>); "their folly" (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.13">Psa 49:13</reference>). He himself, and all, shall at last perceive he was not the wise man he thought he was. <div eID="gen17750" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 11. partridge-- ( 1Sa 26:20 ). Hebrew, korea, from a root, "to call," alluding to its cry; a name still applied to a bustard by the Arabs. Its nest is liable, being on the ground, to be trodden under foot, or robbed by carnivorous animals, notwithstanding all the beautiful manoeuvres of the parent birds to save the brood. The translation, "sitteth on eggs which it has not laid," alludes to the ancient notion that she stole the eggs of other birds and hatched them as her own; and that the young birds when grown left her for the true mother. It is not needful to make Scripture allude to an exploded notion, as if it were true. Maurer thinks the reference is to Jehoiakim's grasping cupidity ( Jr 22:13-17 ). Probably the sense is more general; as previously He condemned trust in man ( Jr 17:5 ), He now condemns another object of the deceitful hearts' trust, unjustly gotten riches ( Psa 39:6 ; 49:16 , 17 ; 55:23 ). fool-- ( Pr 23:5 ; Lu 12:20 ); "their folly" ( Psa 49:13 ). He himself, and all, shall at last perceive he was not the wise man he thought he was.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9974"/><div sID="gen17751" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9974"/><hi type="bold">12. throne--</hi>the temple of Jerusalem, the throne of Jehovah. Having condemned false objects of trust, "high places for sin" (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.3">Jr 17:3</reference>), and an "arm of flesh," he next sets forth Jehovah, and His temple, which was ever open to the Jews, as the true object of confidence, and sanctuary to flee to. Henderson makes Jehovah, in <reference osisRef="Jer.17.13">Jr 17:13</reference>, the subject, and this verse predicate, "A throne of glory, high from the beginning, the place of our sanctuary, the hope of Israel is Jehovah." "Throne" is thus used for Him who sits on it; compare thrones (<reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col 1:16</reference>). He is called a "sanctuary" to His people (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.14">Is 8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.16">Eze 11:16</reference>). So Syriac and Arabic. <div eID="gen17751" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9975"/><div sID="gen17752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9975"/><hi type="bold">13. me--</hi>"Jehovah." Though "Thee" precedes. This sudden transition is usual in the prophetic style, owing to the prophet's continual realization of Jehovah's presence.<div eID="gen17752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all that forsake thee--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.73.27">Psa 73:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.28">Is 1:28</reference>).<div eID="gen17753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17754" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">written in the earth--</hi>in the dust, that is, shall be consigned to oblivion. So Jesus' significant writing "on the ground (probably the accusers' names)" (<reference osisRef="John.8.6">Joh 8:6</reference>). Names written in the dust are obliterated by a very slight wind. Their hopes and celebrity are wholly in the earth, not in the heavenly book of life (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.8">Re 13:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.12">20:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.15">15</reference>). The Jews, though boasting that they were the people of God, had no portion in heaven, no status before God and His angels. Contrast "written in heaven," that is, in the muster-roll of its blessed citizens (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.20">Lu 10:20</reference>). Also, contrast "written in a book," and "in the rock for ever" (<reference osisRef="Job.19.23">Job 19:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.19.24">24</reference>).<div eID="gen17754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">living waters--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.2.13">Jr 2:13</reference>). <div eID="gen17755" type="x-p"/>
